strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: the paper convincingly establishes via two in-the-wild experiments (content-farm prevalence study and differential testing on health questions) that unreliable search results are common and materially shift agent behavior, providing solid grounding before introducing the red-teaming framework.

The automated red-teaming pipeline is carefully engineered: a three-stage test generation workflow (scenario envisioning, test design, test instantiation) with explicit time-gap handling, followed by attainability/integrity filtering via differential testing, is a thoughtful design that reduces reliance on costly manual red-teaming.

Extensive empirical coverage: 3 agent scaffolds (search workflow, tool calling, deep research) x 15 backend LLMs (7 proprietary, 8 open-source), yielding a rich and informative comparison, including reasoning vs. non-reasoning models and scaffold-level effects.

Substantial validation effort for the automated components: human-vs-LLM agreement study for the safety evaluator (~95-98% agreement across configurations), and multiple ablations (injection position, per-website token budget, website generator choice, temporal persistence of the unreliable website) that responsibly interrogate the robustness of the testing configuration rather than presenting a single untested setup.

Findings are non-trivial and actionable: the knowledge-action gap (detectors can flag unreliable sites but agents still use them), the limited benefit of reminder prompting vs. filtering defenses, and the CoT-monitoring case study explaining why GPT-5-mini is more resilient add depth beyond a simple leaderboard of ASR numbers.

Ethics, safety, and reproducibility are handled with unusual care: simulation-based (rather than real SEO manipulation) testing is well justified, the paper discusses harms to human annotators, and code/prompts/test cases are released.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/self-bias in the automated pipeline: GPT-4.1-mini simultaneously serves as website generator, safety evaluator, and helpfulness evaluator, and it is also one of the models being red-teamed (and shown to be highly vulnerable), which could raise concerns about consistency of judgments even though a modest human-agreement check (200 samples) is provided.

Coverage is restricted to Google Search via Serper/Jina, and the study explicitly excludes proprietary end-to-end systems (ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, Gemini Deep Research) which are arguably the most widely used real-world search agents; the paper acknowledges this but the omission limits practical relevance of the concrete ASR numbers to production systems.

Benchmark scale (300 cases, 60 per risk type) is modest, and retention rates during curation are very low for two risk categories (Indirect Prompt Injection 6.8%, Harmful Output 6.9%), suggesting the raw generation pipeline struggles to produce valid/attainable cases for these risks, which may bias the final curated subset toward easier-to-construct scenarios within those categories.

The threat model injects exactly one unreliable website per query in an agent-agnostic, non-adaptive manner; while this is a deliberate and reasonable design choice for fairness, it likely underestimates real-world risk from adaptive/stealthy adversaries (the paper's own defense-evaluation section notes detectors succeed mainly because test-case websites lack stealth), somewhat limiting the external validity of the reported ASRs as an upper bound on real risk.

The initial content-farm prevalence estimate (4.3%) relies on a single zero-shot GPT-4.1 judgment without independent validation of its accuracy, which weakens the quantitative claim used to motivate the study even though it is presented only as a preliminary/motivating result.

No comparison against existing human-curated red-teaming benchmarks or prior related work (e.g., Luo et al. 2025) to demonstrate that SAFESEARCH test cases are comparably or more challenging/realistic, making it harder to judge the added value of automation relative to manual approaches quantitatively.

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored threat surface: the safety implications of unreliable search results for LLM-based search agents, distinct from prior work on static RAG safety or narrow indirect-prompt-injection benchmarks.

The two in-the-wild motivating experiments (content-farm prevalence study and Qwen3-8B stance-shift study) provide reasonably concrete empirical grounding for the threat before the main benchmark is introduced.

Broad experimental coverage: three agent scaffolds (search workflow, tool-calling, deep research) crossed with 15 backend LLMs (7 proprietary, 8 open-source), which is a nontrivial engineering effort and yields informative comparative trends (e.g., reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds tend to be more resilient).

Extensive ablations validating red-teaming configuration choices (injection position, per-website token budget, timestamp persistence, website-generator choice, number of search results) and a human-agreement study for the LLM safety judge, which partially supports the internal validity of the ASR metric.
Thorough, self-aware limitations, ethics, and reproducibility sections, including an explicit (if somewhat defensive) discussion of the sim-to-real gap in Appendix E.5.
weaknesses: Ecological validity of the attacks is questionable: the paper itself admits 'stealthiness is not a principle considered in our test case generation,' and the shown examples (e.g., a website literally instructing the agent to print 'INJECTION_SUCCESS', or overtly implausible fabricated regulatory press releases) are far more blatant than realistic adversarial content, likely inflating the headline ASR numbers relative to what a moderately cautious real-world attacker or naturally occurring low-quality page would produce.

The default injection position ('Last', i.e., lowest-ranked result) is used for all headline numbers, yet the paper's own ablation shows the 'First' position yields meaningfully higher ASR (94.6% vs 90.5% for the top model) — the choice to report the less severe setting as the primary result while relegating the more severe, arguably more attention-grabbing setting to the appendix is a framing choice that should be more transparently reconciled with the paper's claims of representativeness.

Heavy reliance on LLM assistants for essentially every stage of the pipeline (test generation, website generation, filtering, safety judging, helpfulness judging) — often using the same or closely related models (GPT-4.1-mini for website generation, safety evaluator, and helpfulness evaluator) — creates risk of circularity and compounding bias that is only spot-checked on 200 responses from 3 of the 15+ backend models, not systematically validated across scaffolds/models.

The aggressive filtering pipeline (retention rates as low as 6.8–6.9% for prompt injection and harmful output) raises concerns that the retained 300 test cases are a highly selected, possibly non-representative subset optimized for 'attainability' against a single baseline model (Qwen3-8B), which may not generalize to the full space of realistic unreliable content.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 trials per test case with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the many percentage-point comparisons across 15 models x 3 scaffolds x 5 risk types that anchor the paper's core claims.

Real-world proprietary search/deep-research systems (e.g., ChatGPT Search, Perplexity) — arguably the most consequential deployed targets given the paper's own motivating example — are explicitly excluded, and only Google Search via a single third-party API (Serper) is tested, undercutting the paper's claim of broad, deployment-relevant coverage.

Methodological novelty is incremental: the core techniques (differential testing for filtering, rubric/checklist-based LLM-as-judge evaluation, simulated content injection) are recombinations of established practices from adjacent literature (e.g., Ruan et al. 2024, Souly et al. 2024, Luo et al. 2025) rather than a fundamentally new red-teaming paradigm, and the paper's main claimed advance over the closest prior work (Luo et al. 2025) is scope/framing rather than a demonstrably superior methodology.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously characterizes a novel, timely, and underexplored threat surface: the safety of LLM-based search agents when exposed to unreliable Internet search results, clearly distinguishing this threat from RAG safety and generic agent safety literature.

The automated red-teaming framework is well-engineered: a structured three-step test generation pipeline (scenario envisioning, test design, test instantiation) coupled with principled quality-filtering criteria (attainability and integrity) that meaningfully improve test case validity, as evidenced by reported retention rates.

Very thorough experimental coverage: three distinct agent scaffolds (search workflow, tool-calling, deep research) crossed with 15 backend LLMs (7 proprietary, 8 open-source) and 5 risk categories, yielding a rich and informative set of comparative findings (e.g., reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds are more resilient, misinformation is the hardest risk to defend against).

Extensive and careful ablation/validation studies in the appendix (injection position, per-website token limits, website-generator choice, temporal persistence of injected content, and human-vs-LLM safety evaluator agreement at 95-98%) substantially strengthen confidence in the soundness of the reported ASR/HS metrics and default configurations.

Ethical treatment is exemplary: the choice of simulation-based (rather than real-world SEO/adversarial) testing is well justified and explicitly designed to avoid harming real users, and the ethics/limitations/reproducibility sections are detailed and transparent, including honest discussion of what the framework does not cover.

The analysis goes beyond a static benchmark to yield actionable, generalizable insights (e.g., search-result count affecting safety, limited efficacy of reminder-prompt defenses, a knowledge-action gap where models can detect but not act on unreliable content), which increases the paper's practical significance for agent developers.
Good reproducibility support: released codebase, full test cases, and all prompts (generation, safety/helpfulness evaluation, filtering) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively small (300 test cases, 60 per risk category); while the framework is scalable in principle, the empirical results are drawn from a modest sample, especially for fine-grained per-risk ASR comparisons.

Proprietary end-to-end search agent products (e.g., ChatGPT Search, Perplexity) are excluded due to accessibility constraints, which is an important real-world gap since these systems are what most end users actually interact with; the paper's claims about "search agents" broadly are somewhat tempered by testing only self-assembled scaffolds.

The threat model explicitly avoids stealthy, agent-tailored adversarial website crafting; the paper's own defense analysis (Section 4.2) suggests detection succeeds mainly against non-stealthy content, implying that the measured ASRs may not represent a worst-case, more sophisticated adversary and could understate real-world risk in some ways.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge components (test generation, website generation, safety evaluation, helpfulness evaluation are all done by GPT-4.1-mini/o4-mini) introduces potential correlated biases between the pipeline's generator and evaluator, only partially mitigated by the reported human-agreement validation on a modest 200-sample check.

Only Google Search (via Serper API) is evaluated as the search backend; the paper acknowledges but does not empirically probe how results might differ with other search services, limiting generalizability of the quantitative findings.

The explanatory analysis of why GPT-5(-mini) is markedly safer (Appendix D) is exploratory/correlational (based on reasoning summaries rather than full CoT) and the authors themselves note it is inconclusive, which somewhat limits the depth of mechanistic insight despite being a highlighted finding.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering 17 backend LLMs (9 proprietary, 8 open-source) across 3 distinct search agent scaffolds (search workflow, tool-calling, deep research) and 5 risk categories, yielding rich comparative findings (e.g., reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds are more resilient).

The threat model is carefully scoped and clearly justified: benign queries, at most one injected unreliable website, agent-agnostic content, and injection restricted to the first search round — all designed to avoid overestimating risk while remaining realistic.

Extensive validation efforts: human agreement study for the checklist-assisted safety evaluator (95%+), integrity/attainability checks via differential testing, and seven separate ablations of red-teaming configurations (injection position, token limits, timestamp sensitivity, generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness, open-source test generators).

Two in-the-wild motivating observations (content-farm prevalence in search results; stance shifts in health queries) ground the study in a real, empirically demonstrated phenomenon rather than a purely hypothetical threat.

Practical, actionable findings for practitioners: reminder prompting is largely ineffective, search-result count affects ASR, filtering defenses only partially help, and there is a demonstrable 'knowledge-action gap' where models can detect unreliability but fail to act on it — these are useful signals for agent developers.

Thoughtful and well-articulated treatment of ethics/safety (simulation-based testing to avoid harming real users via black-hat SEO), and a clear articulation of how this differs from RAG-poisoning threat models in the appendix.
Good reproducibility practices: prompts, dataset details, and configurations are extensively documented in the appendix, and the framework is stated to be open-sourced.
weaknesses: The core methodological idea — injecting a single synthetic unreliable webpage into search results and measuring downstream propagation — is a relatively incremental extension of existing prompt-injection/RAG-poisoning and search-agent red-teaming literature (e.g., Luo et al. 2025, Ou et al. 2025), and the paper's differentiation from these works (agent-level vs system-level, benign vs adversarial queries) is somewhat narrow rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

The entire pipeline (test generation, website generation, safety/helpfulness evaluation) relies heavily on LLM-as-judge and LLM-as-generator components (primarily o4-mini/GPT-4.1-mini), which could introduce systematic biases or blind spots that a 95% human-agreement spot-check on 200 samples may not fully surface, especially regarding subtle safety failures the checklist itself does not anticipate.

Benchmark scale is modest (300 total test cases, 60 per risk category), and two adversarial risk categories (harmful output, prompt injection) had very low retention rates during filtering (6.9%, 6.8%), raising questions about how representative the retained subset is of the broader risk space.

Only a single search service (Google via Serper API) and content-extraction pipeline (Jina Reader) is evaluated; the paper acknowledges this but the generalizability of ASR numbers to agents using other search backends (e.g., Bing, DuckDuckGo, in-house retrieval) is untested.

The default configuration explicitly avoids persuasive website content, yet the ablation shows persuasive content further increases ASR — meaning the headline ASR numbers likely underestimate the severity of the threat under more realistic adversarial conditions, which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'conservative' framing of the threat model.

The paper is extremely long, with the bulk of methodological nuance, robustness checks, and even some key results (e.g., CoT monitoring analysis of GPT-5-mini, benchmark curation details) relegated to a lengthy appendix, making the core contribution in the main text feel comparatively thin and harder to assess standalone.

Proprietary/closed deep-research systems (e.g., OpenAI's actual deep research product) are excluded from evaluation because of API constraints, leaving open whether findings generalize to the most widely deployed commercial search agents that motivated the paper's introduction (e.g., ChatGPT Search).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-studied problem: the safety of LLM-based search agents when exposed to unreliable search results, which is meaningfully distinguished from the better-studied RAG-poisoning literature (Appendix A provides a clear and reasonably convincing conceptual comparison).

The empirical study is broad in scope: 3 agent scaffolds x 17 backend LLMs (9 proprietary, 8 open-source) x 5 risk categories x 300 test cases, which is a substantial amount of experimentation for a single paper.

Extensive ablations are provided (injection position, per-website token budget, website-generator choice, injection timestamp/freshness, injection round in multi-turn tool calling, test-generator choice including an open-source alternative, persuasiveness of injected content), which meaningfully strengthens confidence that the main findings are not artifacts of a single arbitrary configuration.

The authors validate their automated checklist-assisted LLM judge against human annotation (reported ~95-98% agreement) and separately verify that benign (non-injected) responses are rarely flagged as unsafe (ASR_benign ~0.8% on average), which supports that measured ASR differences are attributable to the injected content rather than evaluator noise.

The discussion of limitations, threat model assumptions, ethical considerations, and the rationale for simulation-based (rather than live, real-world) testing is thorough and self-aware, explicitly reasoning about trade-offs versus large-scale user-driven measurement and real adversarial SEO testing.

Several findings are interesting and potentially useful to practitioners: reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds tend to be more robust; reminder-style defenses are largely ineffective while a dedicated filtering model helps more; search-result count interacts with ASR; and a 'knowledge-action gap' exists where models can identify unreliable sources when explicitly asked but still act on them in agentic settings.
weaknesses: The core threat simulation (always appending exactly one LLM-crafted 'unreliable website' into the top-5 real search results, with the website explicitly guided by a checklist describing the target risk) is a fairly artificial and favorable setup for the attacker/tester: it guarantees topical relevance, inclusion in the returned set, and content tailored precisely to trigger the checklist, which may not reflect how real low-quality or adversarial content actually competes for ranking and attention. The paper's own in-the-wild observation found only 4.3% content-farm prevalence among real top-10 results, which is a much weaker base rate than the single-guaranteed-injection design used in the main experiments; the gap between this motivating statistic and the red-teaming protocol is not fully reconciled.

There is a risk of self-referential/circular evaluation: GPT-4.1-mini (or close relatives) is used simultaneously as the website generator, the safety evaluator, the helpfulness evaluator, and the filtering baseline in defense experiments, while also being one of the models under test. This overlapping role assignment is not analyzed for potential bias (e.g., whether ASR patterns partly reflect generator-evaluator model family effects rather than purely agent robustness), despite being a plausible confound given how central this single model is to the entire pipeline.

The paper positions itself against very recent, closely related concurrent work (Luo et al. 2025, Ou et al. 2025, both 2025 preprints), and the claimed distinctions (agent-level vs. system-level, benign vs. adversarial query framing, broader risk coverage) are somewhat thin given the overlapping subject matter; the incremental novelty of the overall framework relative to this fast-moving space is not strongly established beyond scale and automation.

The human validation of the checklist-based safety evaluator is relatively small-scale (200 sampled responses, 2 annotators who are themselves paper authors and plausibly familiar with the checklist design), raising some concern about independence/circularity of the validation rather than a fully blind, third-party inter-rater study.

Exclusion of proprietary, deployed search agent/deep-research systems (e.g., ChatGPT Search, Perplexity) -- which are exactly the systems motivating the paper's opening real-world anecdote -- substantially limits the practical, real-world significance of the benchmarking results, since the paper can only evaluate self-constructed scaffolds around open or semi-open models rather than the production systems end users actually rely on.

Retention rates for test-case generation vary drastically across risk categories (6.8%-31.3%, Table 3), meaning the final 300-case dataset is a heavily filtered, non-uniform sample whose representativeness of 'typical' real-world risk prevalence per category is unclear, despite the quality-filtering module's stated goal of ensuring attainability/integrity.

Table 1 reports ASR/HS values averaged over only 3 trials per test case without any variance or confidence intervals, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of fine-grained comparisons between closely scoring models/scaffolds (e.g., GPT-5 vs. GPT-5-mini, or small gaps across risk categories).

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a timely and under-studied threat surface for search agents (unreliable search results causing unsafe propagation), with real-world incident evidence and two well-designed in-the-wild pilot observations that establish practical relevance before the main study.

Provides a conceptually careful distinction between this threat and RAG poisoning/adversarial attacks, clarifying scope, threat model (benign queries, agent-agnostic single-website injection, lower-bound safety estimate) and why simulation-based testing is an ethically preferable and more systematic alternative to real SEO manipulation or passive large-scale measurement.

Large-scale, carefully orchestrated empirical study: 3 agent scaffolds × 17 backend LLMs × 5 risk categories × 300 curated test cases, yielding clear and interesting findings (scaffold design and backend model both matter; reasoning/deliberative models more robust; misinformation hardest to defend; reminder prompting largely ineffective while filtering helps partially; safety and helpfulness are not inherently at odds).

Extensive and rigorous validation of methodological choices in the appendix (injection position, per-website token budget, injection round, timestamp sensitivity, website-generator choice, use of open-source test generators), plus human-agreement validation of the LLM safety judge (>95%) and an integrity/false-positive check (ASR without injected content near 0%), which substantially strengthens confidence in the measured effect being attributable to the manipulated search results.

Goes beyond benchmarking to provide actionable insights for agent developers (impact of number of search results, defense efficacy, CoT-monitoring case study explaining GPT-5-mini's relative safety, knowledge-action gap), and commits to releasing code/dataset/prompts, supporting reproducibility.

Thoughtful, non-trivial treatment of ethics/limitations (harmless simulation design, disclaimers for offensive content, discussion of gaps such as proprietary systems and single search-service coverage).
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively small (300 test cases, 60 per risk category) and skewed by differential retention rates across risk types (e.g., harmful output and prompt injection retain <7% of generated raw cases), which may bias the composition and difficulty distribution of the final dataset in ways not fully characterized.

The entire evaluation pipeline (test generation, website generation, safety/helpfulness judging) leans heavily on a small set of LLMs (mainly o4-mini and GPT-4.1-mini); although some ablations address generator choice, potential systematic biases of using GPT-family judges/generators when evaluating GPT-family backends (self-similarity or self-preference effects) are not deeply investigated beyond the reported ablations.

Coverage is limited to a single search service (Google via Serper/Jina) and excludes proprietary deployed deep-research/search systems (e.g., ChatGPT Search, Gemini Deep Research) that are arguably the most consequential real-world targets; while justified by lack of access, this limits the direct real-world applicability of the absolute ASR numbers.

The threat model restricts injection to a single unreliable website agnostic to the specific agent and only in the first search round; this conservative design is well-justified for fair benchmarking, but likely underestimates risk against adaptive or stealthier/multi-source attacks, a limitation the paper acknowledges but does not empirically bound.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-judge for the core ASR/HS metrics, despite strong validation, still carries residual risk of evaluator drift or inconsistency across the very large number of model/scaffold/risk combinations, and the paper's human study, while reassuring, is based on a relatively modest sample (200 responses) from only three backend models.

The main paper is dense and offloads a large share of methodological detail, ablations, and qualitative evidence to a lengthy appendix, which, while thorough, makes it harder to assess some key design choices (e.g., full checklist construction process, representativeness claims) without consulting extensive supplementary material.
